title: Agricultural drone application service (fungicide/insecticide passes + cover-crop seeding)
product_service: For-hire drone application of farmer- or retailer-supplied fungicide/insecticide/foliar products on corn and soybeans (July-Aug window), plus late-summer cover-crop seeding into standing crops.
target_customer: Illinois corn/soybean growers (500-5,000 acres), ag retailers/co-ops that subcontract application, seed companies; secondarily specialty crops.
purchase_motivation: Timely application when ground rigs can't enter (wet fields, tall corn), no wheel-track crop damage, faster than booked-up manned aerial applicators; cover-crop cost-share programs.
spending_evidence: Illinois: 71,123 farms, $17.8B farm production expenses (2022) and 881,228 cover-crop acres [C, WS11-S001]; aerial spraying custom rate averaged $13.31/acre in Indiana 2025 (n=18) vs $8.39 self-propelled ground [C, WS11-S006].
representative_operators: Manned aerial applicators and retailer-owned ground rigs dominate (names not researched) [E]
~1,710 unmanned Part 137 certificate holders nationally by mid-2025 per a training-company blog [D, WS11-S007]
revenue_mechanism: Price per acre applied (chemical usually supplied by customer); seeding priced per acre.
typical_transaction_value: ~$11-15/acre application (aerial proxy $13.31 [C, WS11-S006]); jobs of 200-2,000 acres = ~$2.5k-$30k each [E]
direct_costs: Pilot + visual observer/mixer labor, generator fuel/batteries, drone and battery depreciation (short cycle life), liability insurance, truck/trailer, travel.
contribution_profit_note: Per rig per season maybe 8k-15k acres in a ~6-week fungicide window -> ~$100k-$200k revenue before overhead [E, analyst throughput assumption, unverified].
working_capital_note: Paid at completion or net-30 by retailers; revenue concentrated in ~2 summer months; equipment bought months ahead.
sales_cycle: Seasonal: book growers/retailers in winter-spring; jobs called days ahead based on disease pressure.
repeat_purchase: recurring-seasonal: annual fungicide decisions depend on crop prices and disease pressure
acquisition_channels: Farm shows and county extension meetings
customer_accessibility: Buyers are identifiable (county farm lists, retailers) but relationship-driven; an outsider must earn trust; retailers aggregate demand and are the faster channel.
supplier_accessibility: Constrained: FCC put all new foreign-made drones/components on the Covered List (Dec 2025), blocking new DJI models; owned units still legal [C, WS11-S005]. Non-Chinese heavy-lift alternatives costlier/less mature (assumed).
competitive_intensity: high - rapidly growing operator count, manned aerial applicators and cheaper ground rigs ($8.39/acre) [C, WS11-S006; D, WS11-S007]
entry_strategy: Wet-field/late-season rescue capacity sold through 1-2 ag retailers; small/irregular fields and cover-crop seeding that manned aircraft won't prioritize.
licenses: FAA Part 107 remote pilot; 44807/Part 11 exemption petition (>=120 days lead) and Part 137 agricultural aircraft operator certificate via Form 8710-3 [A, WS11-S002]; Illinois commercial pesticide applicator license ($300 multi-year) with Aerial + Field Crops exams and for-hire liability insurance [A, WS11-S003; B, WS11-S004]; UAS registration.
regulatory_barriers: FAA operational validations/RFIs on exemption holders [A, WS11-S002]; pesticide label restrictions on aerial use; drift liability; FCC Covered List equipment risk [C, WS11-S005].
operational_risks: Weather-limited windows, battery logistics, drift complaints near homes/specialty crops, mid-season equipment failure with no replacement models.
financial_risks: Equipment obsolescence/stranding (software-update waiver only through 2029-01-01 [C, WS11-S005]); price compression as operators multiply; weak corn economics reduce fungicide passes.
geographic_constraints: Central/northern Illinois grain counties; must be near customers during window; minimal in Chicago metro.
founder_expertise: Aviation rules, pesticide labels/mixing, agronomy basics, drone maintenance, seasonal crew management.
staffing: 1-2 seasonal pilots/observers per rig; certified applicator(s); hiring seasonal labor in rural areas.
automation_potential: Flight planning/mapping automated by drone software; AI helps scheduling, invoicing, prospecting; field work stays human.
delegation_potential: Moderate: crews trainable, but founder sells relationships and holds certifications early.
scalability: Add rigs/crews; bounded by short seasonal window and regional density.
expansion: Cover-crop seeding, mosquito/public-health spraying, drone sales/service dealership (supply-constrained), scouting imagery.
roic_note: ~$60k-$150k equipment for 2-3 rigs generating $30k-$180k -> ~50-150% if utilization holds [E].
critical_assumptions: Per-acre prices near aerial custom rates hold as operators multiply
8k-15k acres/rig/season achievable
Compliant equipment remains purchasable/serviceable
unanswered_questions: Illinois-specific drone application rates (farmdoc data not obtained)
Insurance premium for for-hire drone applicators
Price and availability of non-Chinese spray drones in 2027
Fertilizer/chemical expense lines for IL (NASS tables 404)
failure_modes: Undercut by retailers buying their own drones
score_rationale: fcf 4: seasonal utilization caps per-rig profit. roic 5: equipment-heavy but quick payback if booked. access 5: retailers as channel. resilience 5: fungicide spend tracks crop prices. entry 4: fast-growing competition. feasibility 5: FAA exemption + IL license within ~6-9 months.
preliminary_verdict: hold - real Illinois demand and obtainable licensing, but seasonality, FCC equipment risk and fast-rising competition compress returns.

title: Grid/zone soil sampling and variable-rate prescription service
product_service: Post-harvest/early-spring GPS grid or zone soil sampling, lab submission, and variable-rate lime/P/K prescription maps.
target_customer: Grain farmers, absentee landowners/farm managers, independent agronomists; ag retailers outsourcing sampling labor.
purchase_motivation: Fertilizer cost control and yield; landlord-tenant fertility documentation.
spending_evidence: IL farm production expenses $17.8B (2022) [C, WS11-S001]; fertilizer line items not obtained (NASS 404). Precision fertilizer application custom rate $7.90/acre (Indiana) [C, WS11-S006].
representative_operators: Ag retailers/co-ops bundling sampling with fertilizer sales [E]
Independent sampling crews (not researched) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-acre sampling fee plus lab pass-through and per-field prescription fee.
direct_costs: Lab fees, UTV/probe depreciation, seasonal labor, fuel, software.
contribution_profit_note: Short fall window limits acres per crew [E].
working_capital_note: Lab fees prepaid; farmer payment on delivery of results.
sales_cycle: Annual, tied to harvest and fertilizer decisions.
repeat_purchase: occasional: each field re-sampled every 2-4 years
customer_accessibility: Farmers reachable but loyal to retailers who give sampling cheaply to win fertilizer sales.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed in principle: commercial soil labs and probe equipment are widely sold (assumed).
competitive_intensity: high - retailers bundle sampling as a loss-leader [E]
entry_strategy: Serve farm managers and landowners who want retailer-independent data.
licenses: None identified for sampling; prescriptions that recommend pesticides not involved [E].
operational_risks: Compressed fall window, frozen/wet soils, sampling quality control.
financial_risks: Low price ceiling; seasonal idle capacity.
founder_expertise: Soil fertility basics, GIS/prescription software (fits tech background).
automation_potential: Prescription generation and reporting are software; sampling labor stays human.
delegation_potential: Good for field work; agronomic credibility founder-held early.
expansion: Tissue sampling, yield-data analytics, drone imagery.
roic_note: Low capital but low profit pool [E].
critical_assumptions: Enough farmers pay for retailer-independent sampling
unanswered_questions: Share of acres sampled by retailers vs independents
score_rationale: fcf 2/scale 3: small seasonal profit pool. entry 3: retailers give it away. feasibility 9: no license. ai 5: prescription/report automation.
preliminary_verdict: reject - retailers bundle it cheaply and the ceiling is small.

title: Independent seed dealership (seed company dealer/sales agent)
product_service: Selling a seed brand's corn/soybean seed to growers as a local dealer, earning commission/discount margin plus agronomic service.
purchase_motivation: Annual seed purchase is mandatory input; dealer relationship, discounts and agronomy support.
spending_evidence: IL: 33,000+ farms grew soybeans; #2 in corn acres (2022) [C, WS11-S001]; seed expense line not obtained [MISSING].
representative_operators: Farmer-dealers for major and regional seed brands [E]
revenue_mechanism: Dealer commission or margin per unit sold (rates MISSING).
typical_transaction_value: Per grower order likely $20k-$150k of seed [E]
contribution_profit_note: MISSING - dealer commission schedules not found.
working_capital_note: Seed company usually finances inventory; dealer may carry receivables for growers (assumed).
customer_accessibility: Very hard for a non-farmer outsider; seed sales run on long personal relationships.
supplier_accessibility: Unknown: dealer appointments controlled by seed companies, typically favoring farmers with networks.
competitive_intensity: extreme - multiple dealers per township plus retailer seed sales [E]
entry_strategy: Weak; perhaps a challenger brand seeking new territory.
licenses: Illinois seed labeling/dealer permits may apply (not verified) [MISSING].
financial_risks: Grower receivables if dealer extends credit.
automation_potential: CRM and plot data; core sale is relational.
roic_note: Low capital, but low and slow profit [E].
critical_assumptions: A seed company would appoint a non-farmer dealer
score_rationale: access 2/entry 2: relationship-locked market for an outsider. delegation 3: relational. resilience 7: seed is a must-buy.
preliminary_verdict: reject - outsider cannot access relationship-locked grower base.

title: Precision-ag aftermarket hardware dealer + installation/in-season support
product_service: Selling and installing aftermarket planter controls, guidance/autosteer, yield monitors and sensors; winter installs and in-season troubleshooting.
target_customer: Mid/large grain farms upgrading existing equipment instead of buying new.
purchase_motivation: Yield gains/input savings; cheaper than new machinery; urgent downtime support during planting.
spending_evidence: No IL spending data obtained [MISSING]; IL farm count/expenses only [C, WS11-S001].
representative_operators: Independent precision dealers and equipment dealerships' precision departments [E]
revenue_mechanism: Hardware margin + install labor + support subscriptions.
direct_costs: Hardware COGS, technician labor, service truck, demo inventory.
contribution_profit_note: Hardware margins thin; labor is the profit pool [E].
working_capital_note: Inventory and demo units; seasonal cash swings.
repeat_purchase: occasional: upgrades every few years plus support
customer_accessibility: Moderate-low for outsider; dealers' trust built on in-season reliability.
supplier_accessibility: Unknown: manufacturer dealer territories may be filled.
competitive_intensity: high - OEM dealerships with precision staff [E]
entry_strategy: Technical depth and rapid in-season response in underserved counties.
financial_risks: Farm-income downturn cuts capex; inventory obsolescence.
automation_potential: Remote diagnostics; AI support chat; installs stay manual.
critical_assumptions: Dealer appointment available
failure_modes: Capex freeze in weak farm years
score_rationale: resilience 4: farm capex is cyclical. cash 4: inventory. access 3: relationship barrier.

representative_operators: Local bin-service contractors (not researched) [E]

licenses: OSHA grain handling rules apply to employers (citation not verified here) [E].
automation_potential: Bin robots reduce entry; scheduling software.
critical_assumptions: Farmers will pay vs self-perform
score_rationale: fcf 2/scale 2: seasonal niche. cash 7: paid on completion.
preliminary_verdict: reject - small seasonal niche with high safety liability.

title: Commercial electricity procurement brokerage (ICC-licensed ABC) with gas add-on
product_service: Competitive RFPs among licensed retail electric suppliers (ARES) for business customers, contract structuring (fixed/index/block, capacity pass-through), renewal management and bill monitoring; natural gas brokerage as add-on.
target_customer: Small/mid commercial and industrial accounts in ComEd and Ameren territories (manufacturers, multi-site retail, cold storage, property managers, nonprofits).
purchase_motivation: Rising supply costs: PJM capacity cleared at the price cap for 2026/27 ($329.17/MW-day) and 2027/28 ($333.44, incl. COMED) [A, WS11-S020]; budget certainty; time savings.
spending_evidence: Customer choice exists in Ameren, ComEd and MidAmerican territories [A, WS11-S025]; capacity cost shock [A, WS11-S020]. Number of switched commercial accounts and broker market share MISSING.
representative_operators: ICC maintains a public list of certified ABCs (not counted) [A, WS11-S023]
National energy brokers/consultancies (not researched) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Supplier-paid commission embedded in the contract price (per-kWh adder), usually paid monthly over the contract term as the customer consumes; occasionally upfront.
typical_transaction_value: Illustrative: 1,000 MWh/yr account x $0.002-0.005/kWh adder = $2k-$5k/yr for a 2-3 yr term [E - commission rates not verified]
direct_costs: Sub-agent splits, pricing-platform/CRM software, E&O insurance, $5,000 license bond premium.
contribution_profit_note: Near-pure margin per account once signed; value = book of residuals [E].
working_capital_note: Commissions lag consumption by ~30-60 days; clawback risk if customer defaults or supplier fails; no inventory.
sales_cycle: 1-3 months per account; renewals timed to contract expiry.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: 1-3 yr supply terms with renewal
acquisition_channels: CPA and commercial property manager referrals
Bundling with bill audit (WS11-010) and DR (WS11-008)
customer_accessibility: Many identifiable buyers via public business data; decision makers reachable, but heavily solicited by brokers.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed: ARES broker programs common; supplier appetite for small-broker channel not verified.
competitive_intensity: extreme - many licensed brokers and supplier direct sales [E]
entry_strategy: Analytical procurement around the capacity-price shock (PLC/capacity pass-through, DR revenue stacking) plus transparent fee disclosure; target mid-size C&I underserved by big consultancies.
licenses: ICC ABC license under 220 ILCS 5/16-115C / 83 IAC 454: no fee, $5,000 bond, managerial/technical/financial requirements, 90-180 day review, annual report Mar 31 [A, WS11-S023, WS11-S024]; ABC license does not cover gas [A, WS11-S023] (gas broker rules MISSING).
regulatory_barriers: Part 454 technical requirement needs individual(s) with electric-industry experience (years MISSING) - founder may need a hire/partner; consumer-protection rules (Parts 412/453) if serving small commercial [A, WS11-S023].
operational_risks: Supplier credit events; mis-sold index products; reputation in a telemarketing-heavy niche.
financial_risks: Commission clawbacks; churn at renewal; supplier commission cuts; regulatory change (new Illinois grid legislation noted by IPA [B, WS11-S045]).
geographic_constraints: Illinois deregulated territories; expandable to other retail-choice states with separate licensing.
founder_expertise: Tariffs, PJM capacity mechanics, contract structures, supplier relationships, consultative selling.
staffing: Commission sales reps and an analyst after book reaches ~$10k/mo [E].
automation_potential: AI/software for bill and interval-data parsing, load profiling, RFP generation, renewal alerts - real and cheap; selling stays human.
delegation_potential: Good once process documented; book is transferable.
scalability: Residual book compounds; hire reps; multi-state.
expansion: Bill audit, DR enrollment, PLC management, solar/storage referrals, municipal aggregation consulting.
roic_note: <$15k at risk; any book above ~$50k/yr implies >300% [E].
critical_assumptions: Supplier commissions of a few tenths of a cent per kWh are available to new brokers
Founder can satisfy Part 454 technical experience via hire/partner
Capacity-cost shock raises willingness to engage brokers
unanswered_questions: Typical commission rates and payment terms in IL
failure_modes: Regulatory crackdown on broker fee disclosure
score_rationale: roic 9: near-zero capital, recurring residuals. entry 3: crowded. feasibility 5: ICC license with experience requirement and 3-6 month review. ai 6: bill/interval analytics materially reduce analyst cost. Economics unverified (E).
preliminary_verdict: advance - asset-light recurring commissions in a deregulated state with a fresh capacity-cost shock; must verify commission rates and Part 454 experience rule.

title: Demand-response enrollment (channel partner to PJM curtailment service providers)
subindustry: Demand response / virtual power plant origination
product_service: Identify C&I sites with curtailable load or backup generation in ComEd, assess kW potential, enroll them with a CSP (e.g., Voltus/CPower) and manage event performance; earn revenue share.
target_customer: Manufacturers, cold storage, water/wastewater plants, data/telecom sites with generators, large retailers (>=100 kW curtailable).
purchase_motivation: New revenue: PJM capacity at $333.44/MW-day for 2027/28 (~$121.7k per MW-year arithmetic) [A, WS11-S020]; COMED cleared the most DR of any zone (1,515.9 MW) [A, WS11-S020].
spending_evidence: DR cleared in PJM 2027/28 ~7,800 MW UCAP [A, WS11-S020]; CSPs run partner programs with revenue-share/fixed/upfront models [D, WS11-S021]; NRG acquired CPower [D, WS11-S022].
representative_operators: Voltus [D, WS11-S021]
CPower (NRG) [D, WS11-S022]
Enel X and other CSPs (not researched) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Revenue share of customer's DR payments or per-MW origination fee from CSP (rates MISSING).
typical_transaction_value: Illustrative: 500 kW site x $333.44/MW-day x 365 = ~$61k/yr gross capacity value; partner share perhaps 5-15% = $3k-$9k/yr [E]
contribution_profit_note: Recurring per delivery year while site stays enrolled [E].
working_capital_note: Capacity payments flow over the delivery year; partner paid after CSP is paid - long lag (assumed).
sales_cycle: 2-6 months; enrollment deadlines tied to PJM delivery years.
customer_accessibility: Identifiable via manufacturer lists; requires operations buy-in to curtail.
supplier_accessibility: Partner programs exist [D, WS11-S021]; terms for a new small partner unknown.
competitive_intensity: high - CSP direct sales teams and brokers bundle DR [E]
entry_strategy: Local, hands-on site assessments in ComEd zone during the capacity-price spike; stack with procurement and PLC services.
licenses: None identified for referral; ABC license only if also procuring supply [A, WS11-S023]. MISSING: whether PJM/ICC rules regulate DR marketers.
regulatory_barriers: PJM rule changes: DR availability expanded to all hours [A, WS11-S020]; cap/floor applies only to 2026/27-2027/28 [A, WS11-S020].
operational_risks: Customer non-performance penalties reduce payments; churn after a painful event.
financial_risks: Capacity prices could fall after 2027/28; revenue-share terms set by CSP.
geographic_constraints: PJM ComEd zone (northern IL); Ameren is MISO (different market).
founder_expertise: PJM capacity/DR rules, industrial load assessment.
automation_potential: Interval-data screening for curtailment potential is software-friendly.
scalability: Bounded by CSP terms and zone size; multi-market possible.
critical_assumptions: CSPs pay meaningful shares to small partners
Capacity prices stay elevated beyond 2027/28
unanswered_questions: Whether a partner can register as its own CSP later and capital/credit needed
score_rationale: entry 5: structural opening from capacity spike. resilience 4: market-rule dependent. cash 4: long payment lag. Best as bundle with WS11-007.
preliminary_verdict: advance - as a bundle component with brokerage; partner economics must be verified.

title: Capacity-tag (PLC) peak-alert and load-management service for C&I
product_service: Forecast PJM system peak hours, alert customers and coordinate load reductions to lower next year's capacity obligation; savings verification.
target_customer: C&I customers in ComEd zone whose supply contracts pass through capacity costs.
purchase_motivation: Capacity at $333.44/MW-day means each 100 kW of tag reduction ~ $12.2k/yr avoided (arithmetic) [A, WS11-S020].
spending_evidence: Capacity price data [A, WS11-S020]; PJM 5-coincident-peak tag methodology assumed, not verified in this session [E].
representative_operators: CSPs, brokers and suppliers offer peak alerts (not researched) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Monthly subscription or share of verified savings.
working_capital_note: Savings show up the following year; contingency fees lag 12+ months.
customer_accessibility: Only customers with capacity pass-through benefit; need education.
competitive_intensity: moderate - often given free as a broker/CSP add-on [E]
entry_strategy: Better forecasting + hands-on curtailment playbooks; bundle rather than stand-alone.
founder_expertise: Load forecasting (fits tech background), PJM rules.
automation_potential: Peak forecasting and alerting are highly automatable at low cost.
scalability: Software-like but niche; free competing alerts cap price.
critical_assumptions: Customers' contracts pass capacity cost through
Peak forecasting adds value over free alerts
unanswered_questions: Share of ComEd C&I load on pass-through contracts
score_rationale: ai 7: forecasting is genuinely automatable. scale 3: niche, often bundled free.
preliminary_verdict: hold - fold into WS11-007 as differentiator rather than stand-alone business.

title: Utility bill audit and rate optimization on contingency (electric, gas, water/sewer, waste)
product_service: Audit 24-36 months of utility/waste invoices for billing errors, wrong rate classes, tax exemptions, meter/estimated-read errors and sewer credits; file refund claims; optimize tariffs; ongoing monitoring.
target_customer: Multi-site SMBs, manufacturers, school districts, municipalities, churches/nonprofits, property managers.
purchase_motivation: Found money with no upfront cost; budget pressure from rising energy costs [A, WS11-S020].
spending_evidence: Contingency cost-reduction networks operate at scale (Schooley Mitchell claims 350+ offices; fee = portion of savings) [D, WS11-S047]; asset-light waste management broker comp shows ~17% gross margin on pass-through spend [A, WS11-S013].
representative_operators: Schooley Mitchell (franchise network) [D, WS11-S047]
Other national cost-reduction/utility audit firms (not researched) [E]
revenue_mechanism: % of refunds recovered and of 12-36 months of future savings.
typical_transaction_value: $1k-$20k per engagement; often 30-50% of recoveries [E - unverified]
direct_costs: Analyst time, data extraction software, sub-referral fees.
contribution_profit_note: High per hit, but hit rate per audited client unknown [E].
working_capital_note: Fees contingent and lagged until utility issues credits (often 2-9 months); disputes possible.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks to sign; months to collect.
customer_accessibility: Easy yes because no-cost; harder to get complete bill data.
supplier_accessibility: N/A (data comes from client's utility accounts).
competitive_intensity: high - franchise networks and national auditors [D, WS11-S047]
entry_strategy: Software-driven tariff analysis for Illinois utilities; local municipal/school focus; bundle with procurement.
licenses: None for auditing; procuring supply for clients requires ICC ABC license [A, WS11-S023].
regulatory_barriers: Low; contract clarity on savings definitions.
operational_risks: Low hit rate; savings disputes; utility refund limitation periods.
automation_potential: Strong: OCR/LLM bill extraction and tariff comparison cut audit cost; affordable post-2026 with ordinary APIs.
scalability: National possible; growth through reps/channel partners.
roic_note: Minimal capital; ROIC very high if hit rate adequate [E].
critical_assumptions: Recoverable errors exist in enough Illinois accounts
Clients sign 30-50% contingency
unanswered_questions: Typical error rates/refund sizes for IL utilities
Utility refund look-back limits under ICC rules
score_rationale: roic 8: near-zero capital. cash 4: lagged contingent fees. ai 7: invoice analytics durable and cheap.
preliminary_verdict: advance - pairs naturally with WS11-007; verify hit rates and fee norms.

Ameresco [A, WS11-S015]

title: Commercial & community solar O&M (inspections, preventive maintenance, vegetation management)
product_service: Scheduled PM (inverters, combiner boxes, torque checks), drone thermography, module cleaning, corrective repairs, and site vegetation management for community/C&I solar arrays.
target_customer: Independent power producers/asset owners and developers of Illinois community and C&I solar; schools with solar.
